https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/ce97.text: Image source, Kevin Carter/Getty Images Image caption, American Airlines Flight 2398, an Airbus A321 like the plane pictured here, landed safely at Dallas Forth Worth airport By Mallory Moench Published 22 August 2026 One person has received medical treatment after a passenger's laptop caught fire on an American Airlines flight. The pilot had reported a "cabin fire in the back of the airplane" to air traffic control, saying "the flight attendants are trying to put it out now", according to audio obtained by the BBC's US reporting partner CBS News. "I think we have about four to five passengers that were burned by the laptop. The laptop is contained about mid-aircraft." One passenger received medical attention on site and was released after American Airlines Flight 2398 - coming from Atlanta, Georgia - landed at Dallas Fort Worth International Airport in Texas on Friday. The airline told the BBC that the flight landed safely "after reports of smoke from a customer's device during landing. We thank our crew for their professionalism and swift response to quickly contain the device." After landing, the aircraft taxied to the gate, and emergency personnel met the aircraft upon arrival, per procedure. The Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) warns that lithium batteries, including laptop batteries, are capable of overheating , external "as a result of various factors, including if the battery is damaged, overheated, exposed to water, overcharged, or improperly packed". The FAA recorded , external 58 verified lithium battery air incidents so far this year involving smoke, fire or extreme heat. In the last 20 years, the highest number of incidents was related to battery packs, with 84 cases related to laptops. Lithium batteries must be stowed in carry-on baggage only, the US regulator says. In May, a UK-bound EasyJet flight from Egypt was diverted to Rome after a power bank was found to be charging in a passenger's luggage in the hold of the aircraft. The flight was rescheduled for the next day. The UK's aviation regulator the Civil Aviation Authority has said power banks are causing a growing number of serious issues on flights worldwide, and urged more awareness as portable chargers carry "serious risks" of overheating or catching fire. Poland's bishops have condemned surrogacy as commercial services seek to expand in the country. "Surrogacy is by its nature evil and incompatible with Christian faith and morality," the bishops' bioethics committee said. "The desire to have children cannot be interpreted as a right to have children, because a child, in the ontological sense, as a human being, is not the property of its parents." The bioethics committee of the Polish Bishops' Conference issued a statement on Aug. 27 signed by the head of the committee, Auxiliary Bishop Józef Wróbel of the Archdiocese of Lublin. The committee warned that the "conception and birth of a child cannot be the subject of a commercial transaction" between those who offer their body for rent and those who want to obtain offspring in this way. The committee underscored that the practice of surrogacy cannot, therefore, "be tolerated, permitted, accepted, or, even less so, promoted by state institutions." The statement noted that "more and more offers are emerging in Poland guaranteeing the birth of a healthy child through surrogacy," likely a reference to an event organized in the Polish capital, Warsaw, for Sept. 12-13 by the Ukrainian fertility clinic BioTexCom: Center for Human Reproduction. The company says it has a "wide database of donors who meet all individual requirements of clients" as well as "the latest techniques" to achieve "positive results" of in vitro fertilization. BioTexCom describes surrogacy "as a program during which a healthy woman carries a child for the infertile couple" and promises "best surrogate mothers," lower prices, and better services than other medical centers in Europe. However, the bioethical experts of the Polish episcopate pointed out that surrogacy is available only through artificial insemination, usually performed through in vitro fertilization, which has a variety of "genetic, developmental, and psychological" consequences. Moreover, the experts said such "conceived children will be killed through eugenic abortion if genetic or developmental disorders are detected," stressing that "the murder of an unborn child is always an extremely evil act" and that under "law in force in Poland, it is also a crime." The bioethicists said conducting surrogacy outside Poland does not make it legal, adding that it rather resembles "international human trafficking, which cannot be justified either by the desire to have offspring or the consent" of the parties involved. The experts concluded that children are "treated as commodities and not as endowed with an inalienable dignity attached to their humanity." Thus, they called for "the state authorities to take immediate and decisive action to prevent surrogacy by Polish citizens and to block" companies that "offer such procedures." Some analysts noted that Poland lacks surrogacy limitations, unlike Slovakia and Italy, where the practice is banned.
